title: Poached Salmon
subtitle: Gently poached whole salmon fillet with herb butter
excerpt: Salmon fillets poached in a court bouillon of wine, aromatics, and water until just cooked through: silky, pale pink, and nothing like the boiled grey results of overcooking. Served with a simple parsley butter or cucumber sauce.

recipe.sourceNotes: Poaching fish in a court bouillon, a brief aromatic broth, is one of the classical French techniques for cooking delicate fish without fat. In British cooking, poached salmon has been a centrepiece of summer entertaining and cold buffets for more than a century. Salmon was historically plentiful in British rivers; the dish was associated with celebration and formal dining throughout the Victorian and Edwardian eras. It is one of the gentlest ways to cook salmon and preserves its texture better than dry heat.

recipeTools.notes: Wide enough to hold the fillets in a single layer, with a lid.

content.text: The liquid should barely simmer: small bubbles breaking the surface, not rolling boil. Aggressive boiling makes salmon tough and grey. Lower the fillets into the liquid and cover with a lid. The fillets are done when they just flake when pressed gently and the flesh has turned from deep pink to pale pink all the way through. Pull them out a moment before they look done: residual heat finishes the job.
Combine the wine, water, bay leaves, peppercorns, shallots, and parsley sprigs in a wide pan. Bring to a simmer and cook for 5 minutes to infuse.

Lower the salmon fillets into the liquid skin-side down. The liquid should just cover the fish; add a splash more water if needed. Bring back to the gentlest simmer. Cover and cook for 8 to 10 minutes depending on thickness, until the flesh is opaque but still very moist. Remove carefully with a spatula.
Make the herb butter: beat together the softened butter, chopped parsley, lemon zest, and half the lemon juice. Season with salt. Serve a slice on each warm salmon fillet.
